metadata.title: There's No REST API Here.
metadata.subtitle: The Linear API Skill
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: when you point Claude at Linear's API for the first time, where do you actually send a call, and how do you tell it worked? Lands the carry-out that there's one GraphQL endpoint, not many, and neither a 200 nor a 400 tells you the truth by itself.

beats.narration_text: You'd expect Linear to look like every other issue tracker — a REST endpoint per shape of thing. It doesn't. One GraphQL endpoint carries everything. So how do you actually call it with Claude?

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. One URL: POST to api.linear.app slash graphql. Reads are queries, writes are mutations, same endpoint for both. That's the design — one shape over many — and it means REST's status-code intuition stops working here. Two ID systems live side by side: a UUID, which every operation requires, and a human-readable identifier like ENG-123, which only works for reads. Pass the readable one where a mutation expects a UUID and you get INVALID_INPUT back. The Authorization header is the giveaway this isn't REST — the key goes in raw, no 'Bearer' prefix. And an HTTP 200 doesn't mean it worked. GraphQL returns 200 for most errors, with the real failure sitting in the body under dot-errors.

production_viz.label: ONE ENDPOINT, TWO ID SYSTEMS
production_viz.caption: HTTP 200 can still mean it failed — check .errors

beats.narration_text: A handful of patterns keep this manageable. Start with the viewer query — the cheap sanity check that returns who you're authenticated as; if that fails, nothing else will. Before you create or update anything, look up the UUIDs you'll need: a team's UUID for a new issue, a workflow state's UUID to move one along. Description and comment bodies are just Markdown — nothing fancier. And the mutation response carries its own success field, separate from the HTTP status and separate from dot-errors. That's three places to check for a single call — the price of trading REST's fixed shape for GraphQL's flexible one. One more quirk: most connections don't hand back a total count. To know how many issues sit on a team, you paginate and count, or read an aggregate field instead.

production_viz.label: VIEWER FIRST, THEN UUID
production_viz.caption: Markdown body · no totalCount except search

beats.narration_text: Here's the one that catches people coming from REST. Linear's rate limit doesn't come back as a 429 — it comes back as HTTP 400, with an error code of RATELIMITED buried in the body. Same status a broken query returns. So a retry loop written to watch for 429 never fires; it can't tell 'you're throttled' from 'your query is wrong.' And when you do read the reset time, it's in epoch milliseconds, not seconds — divide by a thousand or the wait comes out a thousand times too long.

One endpoint, not many. And neither a 200 nor a 400 tells you the truth by itself — a 200 can still mean it failed, and a 400 can just mean you're throttled. The status code isn't the answer here; the body is.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: show me the GraphQL query I'd send to list my open issues in Linear, and the mutation to move one to 'In Progress,' using real field names and IDs. For each one, tell me exactly what I'd check in the response to know it actually worked — not just that the HTTP status came back 200. Then tell me what changes about that check if I've been rate-limited. Go deeper: ask the same model to write the retry loop I'd wrap around those calls, given that a 400 might mean my query is broken or might just mean I'm throttled — and given that the reset time comes back in epoch milliseconds.
